utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll have appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honour, my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio, assisted by Laura Greer, our intern, and Alma Imamovic, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, good morning to the colleagues from the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. I'm Vasvija Vidovic and together with Nicholas Robson I'm representing Mr. Delic and together with us is our legal assistant Lejla Gluhic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Before we come to you, good morning, sir, we'll come to you just now. Just one or two points. I realise I did not even bring it with me. This morning on my in tray there was communication from the Italian government. It's all in Italian, I don't understand a word of what they say, and unfortunately I didn't bring it and would have had the benefit of Judge Lattanzi's presence here to tell us what it says. But I will make sure that in the next break I bring it with me. That's the one thing. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President. I also received some correspond from the Italians last evening. I don't know if it the same. I do have copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suspect so, because mine is -- it is addressed to you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It is four pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Something like Tahto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I do have some copies if you'd like those distributed now or we can wait until the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you can distribute them now, I would appreciate it very much, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There's one copy for Defence and three for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At least one for Judge Lattanzi. Okay. That was the little point. The next point is that exhibit 1353, that was the map yesterday that the witness was making markings on, and he made three markings and then later made two more that came five. Apparently because of the technical problem that we had yesterday just around that time, the last two markings four and five have not been -- have been deleted or something like that. And the request is we should get the witness to make those markings again and then remove the exhibit that is already in on which the two markings are deleted. I don't know how that is going to be done, whether it is going to be done during cross-examination or during re-examination, I don't know. Any -- yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have solved that problem. I have brought some hard copies of maps with me today that are better representative of the area and I think we'll just proceed with a different map. So we will just keep that as an exhibit as it is if that's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it is not a proper exhibit now because the transcript talked about five places to be marked but it shows only three marked on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Well, then I will ask the witness to re-mark those two other places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you will, thank you very much, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I do that at the appropriate time and not at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Do that when it can be convenient. Okay. Thank you very much. Good morning, sir, and let me just remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else by the truth, okay. Thank you very much. Madame Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karahasanovic.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you some further questions this morning about the 11th of September 1995 and when you were at Kesten. Now, sir, if this had been a normal situation, in other words, the persons had not taken the prisoners, can you tell us what the normal procedure would have been in terms of transporting the prisoners, by whom and to where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interpreting immediately. Your Honour, in the first part of the question it was put to the witness, "I'm going to be asking you further questions this morning about the 11th of September, 1995, and when you were at Kesten." I just want it noted for the record that the witness said that he was at Kesten on the 10th of September and all of the evidence that he gave yesterday related to the 10th of September. I just wish to point that out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, I apologise. The 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The 11th of September was on the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, could you tell us what the normal procedures would have been in the instance when there was a capture of enemy soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if enemy soldiers are taken prisoner I as the assistant commander for security, the first thing that I should do was to search them if they hadn't been searched before to check whether they had any weapons or anything concealed on their persons. I was supposed also to take their documents, personal IDs that I could then collate with the formation that they provided me with. I would ask them for their full names and I would make a list in my notebook or a piece of paper or anything, and after that if I had enough time and if I was dealing with a smaller number of people I would ask them about their unit, where they were deployed, what they were doing, things like that. After this questioning on my part and before all this, it would be my duty to report to the military police in the brigade to tell team that we had prisoners so that they could come and take over those prisoners from me, take them to the brigade, where they would face further questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where was the military police located, the brigade military police?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade military police was in Zavidovici because the brigade command was in Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: In fact, on this day, didn't you in fact make a request for the military police to bring a truck to pick up the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did that, through my commander. I notified my commander that we needed assistance, that we needed means of transport for the prisoners to take them from that location, because the distance between Zavidovici and Kesten was too big for them to go there on foot, so a vehicle, an appropriate vehicle was supposed to come to Kesten, pick them up, and take them there. And my commander then notified the assistant commander for security, the assistant commander for security notified his commander in turn and it was their duty to notify the police because it was his demand to the military police to go there and to pick those prisoners up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you know if that demand was made? In other words, were you told that, yes, the police -- military police had been telephoned and a truck is on its way?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I was in Kesten until night-fall. The military police did not come, the truck didn't come. They had already learned that the prisoners of war had been taken away, and probably they thought there was no need for them to go to Kesten or maybe there was some other reason for their failure to appear, but at any rate, neither the military police nor the truck ever appeared in Kesten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with regard to the three Serbian women, you said on direct examination that the last time you saw these women they were being escorted by a soldier, moving from Kesten to Malovan Greda on the footpath. Is that what you -- is that what your testimony was?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, if you know, who was at the command in Marici to receive these women?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some officers there from the battalion, for instance and they would have received them, because the commander himself was at the battalion. Ahmet Sehic, the battalion commander. And he was in a position to receive them and wait for our arrival and then we would have taken in their information, but since I only passed them by, we just exchanged a couple of words, I told him, Are you taking them to the battalion command? Wait for us there until we come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now after the Arabs took the other POWs did you called commander Sehic to -- to discuss the women? In other words, the women are walking along this footpath. Were you concerned about the women once the men were taken away?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander -- after this incident, the commander also came to Kesten. I spoke to him, and he relayed to me this information before the soldier did, but I did ask the soldier because he took over from the company commander those captive women, and he was leading them away. When I came to Marici to check what had happened, I asked the soldier, What had happened to the women, where did you take them to, what happened, and he told me the things that I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, how long was it from the time you saw the women to the time you first saw the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately half an hour, something like that. Because the time it took me to get down there, I was probably halfway there. It was downhill. It may have taken me about ten minutes to get to Kesten, then the making of the list that I described yesterday. I think half an hour, 35 minutes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And now -- at the time that you saw the women, how long would it have taken them to get to Marici on the footpath?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, 30 to 35 minutes, something like that. That's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So technically at the time you saw the women, they should have arrived in Marici at the same time you arrived at the Kesten hall.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would have been a bit later for them. I arrived at Kesten before they did, because their trip was longer because I was able to go downhill to Kesten from the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I'm corrected. About the same time that you saw the Arabs would have been the same time had they been walking straight to Marici that they would have arrived there. In other words, it was half an hour before you saw the Arabs, and it would have taken them a half-hour to walk to Marici. So something happened between the time you saw the Arabs and you don't know any details about what happened?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there were a number of elements to this last question put by the Prosecution. I'm not sure how the witness is supposed to respond. Perhaps it could be broken down into question by question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. You told us a minute ago that when you saw the women on the footpath, at that point it would have taken them approximately 30 minutes to get to Marici, right? And it took you ten minutes to get to the Kesten hall, approximately?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then approximately 20 minutes later you -- that's approximately when -- the first time when you saw the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So nowhere during this time-period were you ever -- were you ever notified by the soldier or anyone that these women had been taken, were you? You weren't notified of that, at all?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And these women were in the custody of a 5th Battalion soldier, were they not?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you say -- I believe you said yesterday that you were frightened that day when you saw the Arabs with their guns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room where I was, given their behaviour, of course, I was afraid for my own life, the life of my soldiers, and the lives of the prisoners, because they were quite rough. They were yelling, they were brandishing their weapons, training the weapons at us, throwing their weight about. They were just walking around, strutting around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, apart from what you -- what you saw that day, had you heard anything about the behaviour of Arabs or Mujahedin in terms of treatment of prisoners or just in terms of their general behaviour? Did you hear anything negative about them?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything negative about them. I was simply surprised by their behaviour. I didn't expect them to behave the way they did at that time, because I had thought those were normal people, people who behaved normally as we did in the BH army, but on that day, they did not act like normal people at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, do you know if Commander Sogolj saw the Arabs and if anything took place between he and the Arabs, did you ever hear anything or did you ever see anything?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Sogolj, Commander Sogolj commanded a company and Ahmet Sehic was the commander. Who are you interested in now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sogolj. Was he present in Kesten at the same time that you were present?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Kesten when I arrived. That's what I stressed yesterday. He waited for me to get there. He told me what had happened, how it had happened and then he moved on with his unit. He moved away. I remained in Kesten and three or four soldiers. That's what I said yesterday. And Muhamed Omerasevic, the assistant commander arrived later. Those are the people who were in Kesten at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But when you just said that, "He waited for me to get there, he told me what had happened, how it happened and then he moved on with his unit," what did he tell you, what had happened and how it happened, what is that that he told you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he told me that this group had come out of the forest, that they had surrendered to them, that they had taken this group with them, disarmed them, seized the documents and all those documents were in a heap there. He told me that those two men had tried to seize the weapons. That's what I described yesterday. They tried to grab the weapons from our soldiers and they were disarmed, in turn. And this was not the whole company. This was just an element of the company that took them in. I don't know whether these two people thought that they could simply kill all our soldiers and that's what led them to attempt that, but they were killed at the end. The rest were taken to the hall and that's where I came in. And he told me as I've already indicated that four other enemy soldiers had been captured by the Arabs. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So he told you that four other enemy soldiers had been captured by Arabs and did he say where these Arabs were?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some were there in Kesten. He didn't tell me, because when I came, there were no Arabs there. He also told me that they had two children, two underage children and they had let them go, and he told me that they had taken away three women and I said that I had met them on the way down and that I had instructed them to go to the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just break it down, sir, one -- perhaps one point at a time. "He also told me that they had two children, two underage children and they had let them go." This was the ABiH soldiers had two underage children? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were probably Serb children who had surrendered together with the 51 people that I listed, and the three women. So children -- the children were with them and they were let go by the BH army soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That was my question. My question wasn't articulate enough. The soldiers released from their custody those children. That's -- that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, where did the children go to?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as he described it to me, they had gone back into the woods, and as to what happened to them in the end, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, this area around Kesten, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that it had several land-mines, didn't it, and it still does today?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were land-mines laid only between our lines and the enemy lines and in the depth of the enemy territory there were less land-mines because I don't really believe that they would lay mines in the areas where they moved, but between our two lines, the -- our line and the enemy line, that's why land-mines were laid. And once you passed that line you feel safer moving around because you can't image that somebody would actually lay mines in -- that they would do it in their own rear, where they were moving around.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But I have to go back to the point about the underage children. It's not plausible, is it, that the underage children just left and walked into the woods, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's a call for speculation and the witness has told the Trial Chamber what he was told about the children and he said that he didn't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I will put the question a different way.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, you were the assistant commander for security for the 5th Battalion. That means that you were responsible for at the first level of prisoners of war. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was responsible for taking in those prisoners and to transfer them on to the brigade. That's where my responsibility ended. But since it never happened that way, I never handed them over to the brigade. Because of this incident I was unable to do so. I was unable to transfer them to the brigade because the military police did not arrive. Had the military police arrived at the time when the Arabs were in there, that would have been a different story, because there would have been more of those military police and it would not have ended the way that it had ended in the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But -- and you never made any further inquiry about what happened to the underage children, did you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I actually never saw the children. I didn't know who they were. They were from the other side, from Republika Srpska, and I didn't know and I didn't have anyone to ask about them, because I don't know who knew more, who would be in a position to know more about what had happened to them. They were allowed to go. I didn't hear about them being recaptured. I simply didn't have any information about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go back to what Commander Sogolj told you. What -- tell us everything you recall that he told us [sic] about the Arabs that he met or seen.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he simply told me that that morning, in that area, either close to the hall or maybe a bit further away, it's a rather large area, that he told me that they had seen the capture of four Serb soldiers. That's the only thing he told me in this regard. And I simply made this note for the record, so that we know that Arabs had captured those people, because I was supposed to draft this report and I had to put that in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, if these Arabs who captured those four prisoners were not part of the ABiH, then wouldn't you have had to make a report or call for assistance or try to find out what happened to those four soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply can't see who I was supposed to go to, to ask for the information, because they had been take away in the morning before my arrival. That's what I heard about. I didn't see that. How far they could have been taken, whom I was supposed to ask about the identity of these people. It was a war. You cannot conduct an investigation because there is gun-fire all over the place. You simply have to try and keep yourself alive, and as for making any kind of inquiries or investigations, this was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I can understand the situation, sir, and being war and shooting all around you. But, again, you are the assistant commander for security and you learn of four Serb soldiers being taken by Arabs and you don't make a call to commander Malicbegovic or commander Sehic or anyone?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I learned that, I didn't have that because I was not the assistant commander of those Arabs. I did not collaborate with them and I was not in charge of their case. I was in charge of this case or incident that happened in the 5th Battalion and I tried to deal with what had happened in the 5th Battalion and I couldn't process stuff from any other units that were present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Commander Sogolj was the commander of the 2nd Company. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the 2nd Company is in the 5th Battalion, isn't it? It was in the 5th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So ultimately --

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So ultimately those four Serb prisoners were within your jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how they could have been. They were not taken prisoner by my soldiers. Those four Serbs therefore were not under my jurisdiction. Had they been captured by my soldiers they would have been, but since they were captured by some other soldiers, they could not have been under my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So it's fair to say, then, that those other soldiers who captured those prisoners were part of the military, otherwise it would have been a crime for them to just walk away with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The question is: Those Arabs who took those Serbs must have been part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for them to be able to just take those prisoners and walk away without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, it's a call for speculation. The witness can only -- has told the Trial Chamber what he was told by Mr. Sogolj about the events which resulted in four VRS soldiers being taken away, and again, in my submission I don't think it is a proper question to put this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour. I'm trying to find out what his responsibilities were and I think he has made it clear in his position as assistant commander of security for the 5th Battalion he is informed of a situation by a subordinate commander, and I think that the question is a fair question. Wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. The question is allowed. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you want me to re-ask the question, sir, or do you recall the question and can you answer it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the question. How should I know whether those Arabs belonged to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? I don't know what army they belonged to. They could have been a paramilitary formation belonging to no one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The logic of the question is if you didn't know who they were, what did you do to make sure that you re-take the prisoners of war from them because they have now taken people from you for whom you are responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't responsible for those prisoners, as I said. They were taken away by the Arabs. As to where they took them, I don't know. I didn't see that. And my unit did not stop that. I couldn't go and search for the prisoners, where they were and with whom, I had no time or space for that. I based my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have answered, you have answered that. You said they were not your responsibility. That answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So -- so if they were strangers in the AOR of the 5th Battalion who took prisoners of war, then you had no responsibility with regard to that situation. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Delic. Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Not in the presence of the witness, Your Honour, I would object, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. -- I guess if you have something to say, sir, say it to your lawyers. Okay? You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I would like an answer to my previous question, sir.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not within the AOR of the 5th Battalion. They were in the AOR of the 328th Brigade. It comprised several battalions. I don't know from what direction they came. They could have come from the AOR of the 1st, 2nd, or the 4th Battalion, not only from the AOR of the 5th Battalion to be under my jurisdiction. They may have simply gone through Kesten. It needn't necessarily mean that they were within our AOR, maybe they were just passing through. As to where they came from and what was the direction they were going to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, if the 2nd Company commander is telling you about this, did he hear it from a commander of another company or another battalion, or did this happen to him?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who he heard it from or what he saw. He only told me that four Serb prisoners had been taken by the Arabs. I don't know whether he saw that, heard that, or anything of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did he say --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. I would like to clarify something pertaining to your penultimate answer. You said, namely, at page 17, line 11, that it was not the duty of the 5th Battalion to deal with it. After that, it seems as if you were saying, two lines below, that they may have been within the AOR of the 1st, 2nd or the 4th Battalion rather than the AOR of the 5th Battalion alone. This is a somewhat different answer from the previous one. I would like to clarify the following, whether they were or were not within the AOR of the 5th Battalion. Are you absolutely certain of that and did you know anything about it at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were focussing our activity on Kesten and they passed through. I'll try to explain this. They could have come from the area or from the AOR of the 1st Battalion and then just passed through our area or maybe they had taken those people prisoner somewhere else. The person who talked to me told me that he heard or saw that there were four captured soldiers held by the Arabs. As to whether they had been taken prisoner in Kesten or at another elevation, village or location, I don't know. They merely passed through that area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, wasn't it within your competence to check whether those people had been taken prisoner in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't think it was necessary for me to go about checking it and to investigate. As I said, it was -- there was war and we couldn't conduct investigations. You can do that in peacetime but at that time it was impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand now that you didn't see it fit or necessary to determine that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a few more questions before I leave this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did Commander Sogolj tell you, did he ever meet or speak with any of the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when the -- when you first saw the Arabs and you were in the hall -- well, first, let me back up a second. How many -- how many companies are in the 5th Battalion or were in the 5th Battalion?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four companies.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And there are approximately how many men to a company?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 120 or between 100 and 120, depending on whether everyone was there. Some people were absent due to illness or so, but in any case, a company should have had between 100 and 120 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that in the area of responsibility of the 5th Battalion on the 10th of September, there may have been approximately 400 soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The battalion was not deployed at the lines. That is to say, not all of it was there. For example one company was at the lines, another one was ready to go, the third one was on leave, and so on and so forth. I would say that at the lines at any given time within our AOR there were between 100 and 120 soldiers. It never happened that the entire battalion was at the lines or within the AOR at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- but there were other battalions operating alongside the 5th Battalion, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We had the neighbouring units on both sides. The lines of defence were interconnected. There were no gaps. You would have one battalion to the next. They were all linked up and the line was uninterrupted.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, can you explain for us, for myself and the Chamber what those other battalions were, if you can?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th and the 5th.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell -- thank you. That makes sense. Those are the five battalions in the 328th Brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many soldiers all of those battalions -- how many soldiers were -- participated in the operation on the 10th of September?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that we had our own lines and our own axis. I can tell you how many soldiers our battalion had and what -- whether -- the things we were doing. As for the other battalions, I had no opportunity to go there and check, and I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: What my next series of questions or my next question, though, is when this incident happened in the Kesten hall, why didn't you radio the commander of the 5th Battalion or the brigade and ask for assistance from soldiers, other soldiers who were in the area?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did notify the commander. I called him on the phone. When I saw how many prisoners there were, I went out of the hall and I called my commander. I conveyed to him what was going on and I told him that I needed assistance, since it was impossible for me to escort them with the three or four soldiers I had. I needed the military police and a vehicle to transport them. I did notify him.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But assistance never arrived, did it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It never arrived in Kesten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did it arrive anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't go anywhere from Kesten. I was in Kesten and it didn't arrive there. As for whether they arrived anywhere else, I don't know. I couldn't see that, since it is a forested area. There is just a small clearing with a few houses. It's a rather small village, and I couldn't see anything beyond that. It is in a gorge of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But when -- when the Arabs left Kesten hall with the prisoners, they were on foot. Correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And there was no -- no army Bosnia-Herzegovina soldiers ever -- were ever called to your knowledge to come and confront this group of 20 to 30 Arabs?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, the unit had already left. They went further, since they cleared that part of the terrain up, leaving the prisoners behind in the hall. They left behind the basic security that we thought would be sufficient to secure that group of people. However we did not see any of the things that happened subsequently coming. We thought, since we had taken those people prisoner, that they were our prisoners and that they would be sent on to the brigade. However, we didn't know that the things would develop the way they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And when the things developed, sir. I guess I'm puzzled why you had the whole army there fighting a major operation on the 10th of September and there is no, to your knowledge, action taken against 20 or 30 what you've described as Arabs.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We had our troops on the lines and some of them had gone through that territory. As for the other troops, some were at home, on leave, and others were in the other parts of the AOR at the state of ready. We called our commanders. I notified my commander, the assistant commander of the brigade was notified, and they were supposed to send in the military police alongside a vehicle. We didn't have a vehicle to transport the prisoners in.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Operation Farz, though, was a major operation, you would agree with me, and that it actually ended the war, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war did not end with that operation, as far as I know. That operation merely served to liberate the corridor between Zenica and Tuzla and a general area around Vozuca. However, the war was still ongoing. It ended in December 1995, if I'm not mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But the victory of the ABiH on the 10th was a major victory, wouldn't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was a victory. On that day, the army liberated a large part of the territory. As for the issue of victors, we know nowadays that no one won in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to discuss for a moment when the group left, the 20 to 30 Arabs and the prisoners. Now, again, would you agree that this was a dense -- a forest area, mainly, around Kesten?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you would also agree that there were some land-mines in the forest area.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Kesten itself, I think, but further on, if one goes between the lines, that area must have been mined.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And there was combat going on on the 10th of September. As you indicated earlier there was firing going on all around you, right?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So this group of Arabs that took the prisoners, you would agree with me, wouldn't you, that they would have to know the terrain, they would have to know where the land-mines were and they would have to know where the combat operations were taking place in order to just wander off from the Kesten hall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It is a clear call for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm testing the credibility of the witness and what he has testified to with reality, and I think it is a fair question for him to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, would you please answer the question?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that anyone knew what was mined and what wasn't. For example, our AOR was a mystery to us. We didn't know whether there was a minefield in front of us or not. We used paths to stay safe. I don't think anyone in the area knew what was mined and where. We couldn't get our hands on any documents or papers indicating minefields. We moved about trying to stay safe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But certainly you, the army, the units, had equipment and had intelligence information and had knowledge about where to go or not go. Otherwise, it would be chaos. Everyone would just be getting blown up and shot at. So there had to be some sort of information that the soldiers had in order to move about and carry out the operations with regard to land-mines and other combat operations. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we moved to the lines and back we counted on our luck. We tried to assess where minefields could be. In a number of cases our soldiers came upon minefields, they lost limbs, were getting killed by mines. Had we known where the land-mines were, we would not have sent them there. We would have circumvented the fields, but we counted on our luck. There were instances though in which we had soldiers whose limbs were blown off or people were being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Let's move away from land-mines. What about the different operations that were going on being performed by the five different battalions. Each battalion would have to know what was going on in order to avoid cross-fire or being killed by their own soldiers. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. What do you mean not being killed by their own soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You've got -- you're in a war and there's shooting going on. There are five battalions operating during this war in different areas of responsibility. Now, one person from one battalion would have to know the area of where another battalion was operating in order not to enter that area or in order to understand and -- to understand the situation so there's no killing of each other. Isn't it true?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commanders assigned axes. It wasn't me who was doing it. I wasn't responsible to command and control. Commanders would determine the line of action. The line, as I said, was uninterrupted, and we used the line. No battalion went ahead of any others. We moved all together in one particular direction, and it couldn't happen that we were shooting at each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Right. So you would know which direction each other were going sow wouldn't be shooting at each other. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was known, as I said, commanders set up axis. At the level of command they must have agreed on their respective areas in order to liberate the terrain and to carry out searches of terrain in order to arrive at certain locations. I don't know what those were though. I wasn't present at their meetings and wasn't privy to their discussions. It was above my level.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in an area of war, it's not appropriate -- or you would take all precautions to ensure that persons who were not engaged in the warfare such as civilians or random groups would not just be wandering around in the area of combat?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no civilians there. Our villages were away from the lines, and our civilians couldn't have been there. Once combat begins and if there were any civilians on the other side, well, I didn't see any civilians in the villages nearby. It means that they could not have been in any of the places where there was combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the same would apply for any just random group that were not part of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They couldn't just be wandering around in the middle of a combat, could they?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To have a random group. Who do have you in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have in mind the group of Arabs, sir.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How they got there, I don't know, and where from, but they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you would have to agree with me wouldn't you, that they would have to know what was going on in the area in terms of combat in order not to be shot at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, calls for speculation. How could the witness know what was in the minds of the Arabs, what they knew or didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will lay a foundation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. Let me just put my problem to you too. My problem is now you're classifying these Arabs as a random group. They seem to have been armed. They seem to have been part of some kind of army. So they were not just a random group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for correcting that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, any unit in the area of combat would have to know what was going on in order to avoid any type of friendly fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the same objection as before, although now it has been put as any units in the area of combat. Again how can this witness speak for other units particularly when it's been put so vaguely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this gentleman is assistant commander for security and one of his main responsibilities is security of the troops. I think it is a fair question to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio, I don't -- I'm not sure I understand fully how you're going to test the truthfulness and the credibility of this witness but putting these questions, which I would agree with the Defence are quite speculative.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If I just may ask a few more questions and if it doesn't become clear then I will leave this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you doing about that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, and I can bring up your former, your previous statement if you want, but I have a quote here from paragraph 27 of Exhibit 1354 which was a statement you gave on the 18th of September of 2006. You said: "As far as I can remember, I or my unit never had any orders to have any surveillance on El Mujahedin or to follow them closely. They only came to our area of responsibility now and then and it's a -- it's a two-on reconnaissance --" that's what the statement says "-- and so I could not follow them. They only reported into the area and then the soldiers were informed so that nobody shot at them." So, what you said was that when the El Mujahedin came into the area the other soldiers had to be informed so that nobody shot at them. So my question is how would this group of Arabs be able to walk around the area of combat without getting shot at unless someone knew where they were and who they were and they were part of the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It's the same point, Your Honour. Again, it's a call for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Fine, I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to get to the list of names. Now you already told us and I believe you told your commander that there were too many prisoners to handle and that you needed assistance, and you've also told us that you never got assistance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, how long were you in the Kesten hall, before the prisoners were taken away?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, the time it took me to make the list with 51 names and that's how long I stayed in the hall with the prisoners in Kesten, because I stayed there for as long as it took me to make the list. It may have been half an hour, I don't know, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, in -- in a previous statement, you told the investigator it took 15 minutes to take down the names. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember having said that or actually I remember that I told him that it took me as long as it takes one to write down 51 names, years and places of birth. Whether it's 15, 20 to half an hour, 15 minutes, 20 minutes, half an hour, at any rate that's how long I stayed there. I didn't have a watch on me to check how long I actually was in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you weren't there very long, were you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not very long. I made the list and as soon as I -- or actually, after I made the list there was five minutes of the discussion with the Arabs and then after the five minutes quarrel with the Arabs after they forced me to leave the hall, I left the hall and that is the sum total of the time that I spent in the hall.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you never checked the names against the identification that had been confiscated from these prisoners, did you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't check it against documents, but at that time I was not in a position to do so, because the prisoners were taken away. The only thing that I had left was this heap of paper and it would to me no good to check it. But yesterday when I saw the other list, the one that was sent on, I could see that it tallied with my list and that they provided me with the correct information. There were just some really minor discrepancies. They told me the truth because they didn't know what I would do, whether I would check what they told me against their documents. They knew that I had their documents. I would most probably have done that had this incident not occurred.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have a couple of more questions, Your Honours, and then I'd like to take a break and then we can do the map, if that would be okay. Sir, isn't it true that the 5th Battalion had a training facility or a training place at the 9th kilometre school?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion did not have any such facilities. The 5th Battalion had a private family home and on the ground floor there was the office of the battalion commander and the offices of us assistant commanders and the battalion did not have anything at the ninth kilometre. They did not go up there at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- but isn't it true that they were trained by the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 5th Battalion, the troops in the 5th Battalion, when I joined them in early September, the soldiers never went to train with the El Mujahed unit, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And one more question on this. It's true that on several occasions, members of the 5th Battalion were subordinated to the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions on this. If we could take an early break, Your Honour, so I can set the map up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean set it up?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We need to bring it up and I need to look at the places again and ask the witness the appropriate questions in order to redo the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why can't you do that in the next seven minutes before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's bring it up. It is exhibit 1353, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, just to note this is not an exhibit that's been admitted into evidence. It was identified as an MFI document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the map on the screen?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And yesterday I asked you to -- if you could identify two other places on the map. One was Kosa village.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Duga Kosa here. Greda, that's not the village. I don't know. Where do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, if you look to your -- oh, sorry, Kosa is named. Sorry, I apologise for that, it is circled. I asked you where Duga --

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosa is, yes, Kosa is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The place that I asked you about yesterday was Djurica Vis, if could you circle that for us.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then I asked you -- oh, sorry. Could you put a number 4 beside that, please.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And then I asked you to circle Gornja [sic]. If you look up north, sir, you might be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gornjani, not Gornja.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a couple of questions before we leave that -- oh, sorry. Could you mark that as number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We ask that this be admitted in evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object on the same grounds as I did yesterday and the reason is that in respect of numbers 1, 2, and 3, the witness was shown a document yesterday and simply asked to read out the names of three locations on that document. He wasn't asked any questions about those places and no link was established. He then marked those locations on this map as 1, 2, and 3. He is now been asked about two of the locations, Djurica Vis and Gornjani, and again no questions have been asked about those locations. All of us in this courtroom, given time, could have performed that exercise so I fail to see the relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have another map that I'm going to ask the witness to put these places on again that's more clear and then I will ask questions, but I was told I had to do this because of yesterday so I have asked the witness the questions. But I intend to open up that area of examination in more detail using another map. So I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Another map of exactly the same areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To point exactly the same five --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: These five will be on there, yes, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you want him to point those five out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection, Madam Sartorio, is what are we supposed to make of this document. You are saying you are marking four and five today because you've been asked to do so by us. Yes, you are being asked to do so by us because you did it yesterday. Why did you do it yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document illustrates places that the witness has been asked about, to ask him just to identify the places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the objection is anybody who is literate can look at this map and make the circles that the witness made without ever having been on the scene. There have been no questions put to the witness in relation to these places that have you asked him to mark. If you ask me to take this map and mark Gornjani, circle it, I would have circled it too. But I know nothing about Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will just ask that this be marked for identification for the present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is already so marked, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will move on to a series of questions or we can take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will definitely take a break at this stage --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and you can move on to your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the map that was tendered yesterday that -- from which 4 and 5 were deleted will be removed and this one will be taken as MFI 1353. Court adjourned, come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you some questions now about what, if anything, you knew about the operations that took place on the 10th of September, and my first question, which is just setting some foundation is, in September of 1995, the 328th Brigade was subordinated to the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the 5th Corps -- 5th Battalion, excuse me, was subordinated to the 328th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And one of your main duties as assistant commander for security was to maintain the security of the area where the troops were operating. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my duty to take care of my soldiers at the defence line where they were. It was my duty, for instance, if a trench or a dug-out was unsafe, it was my duty to order that the soldiers move out because of the safety of those soldiers. Because if that position was too far forward, it might be targeted by the enemy, by mortar fire and so on. So I was to take care of the safety and security of the soldiers and of the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in order to be able to do that, you would agree that you would have to visit the front line and, in fact, you did visit the front line almost on a daily basis during Operation Farz, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the course of Operation Farz, because there was no defence line during the operation. Once the operation was launched, a line was in motion, but up until Operation Farz, we had a stable line, a line that I visited regularly to see how things were. I said that I had come in in early September, I think somewhere around the 1st of September, that's when I joined the unit. I wasn't familiar with the unit, and in order to acquainted myself with them so that the soldiers knew who their assistant commander for security was and since this was a new line for me, I wasn't familiar with it, I toured the line to see what the situation was like, to see whether my predecessor had done his job properly. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And after having visiting the front line you would normally report on the security of the front line, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would report to my commander if there was any need for any changes to be made, I would speak to the commander either orally or I would submit something in writing, but because we were both in the battalion and we would see each other practically every night, I was able to just tell him such-and-such a thing was not all right, it has to be changed, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you also work fairly closely with your counterpart assistant commanders in the intelligence department for the battalion, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the assistant commanders were there and in the evening, after all the tasks were completed, tasks that either were set to us or that we ourselves decided we would have to do, we would meet up in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you also met frequently with other battalion commanders and exchanged information about the security that they had gathered on their front -- in their areas of responsibility, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the battalion commanders, no. I didn't meet with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, perhaps then if I refresh without bringing up your statement, you did say in a previous statement, quote, that you had -- oh, I apologise, I don't have the quote.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If we can bring it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If you said in your previous statement that you met with other battalion security commanders, is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It is paragraph -- yeah, we can bring up the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson? But -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Exhibit 1354, please, paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I was just going to say it wasn't a proper question and I think in fairness to the witness my learned friend should put to him what he's supposed to have said in the statement so he could comment fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I also would say that your first question, madam, talked about battalion commanders. Now you're talking become battalion security commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. I meant security commanders, assistant security commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when he said he never met with battalion commanders, are you still disputing that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sorry, sir, my question is, did you meet with other battalion assistant commanders for security?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a fair question. I did meet with the assistant commanders for security at the brigade assistant commander for security when we had the monthly briefings. That's where we met, but, otherwise, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you -- did you attend any meetings in preparation of Operation Farz?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only the commanders attended those meetings, not us. I don't know whether the brigade assistant commander for security did attend, but, at any rate, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But I guess I'm curious, how could you perform your duties of maintaining security on the front line if you didn't have -- attend the meetings or -- well, strike that. Did you learn in any other way, by reading orders or speaking with the commander, about what operations were going to take place?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an operation was supposed to take place in the area of responsibility of that brigade, the assistant commanders were not given this information for one reason, lest this information should leak and reach the soldiers. That is why only the battalion commanders would know that. And since we did not participate in combat we only held the defence line. There was no need for us to know that. The commander took care of that, not us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But, so I'll go back to the question I was going to ask. How were you able to maintain security on the front line if you don't know what is going on from an operational standpoint?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I took care of the security of what is already there, because we didn't move anywhere that would enable me to take any other measures. We held a position, that's the position where we were, until this area was liberated and until the unit moved on. And once a unit reaches a certain position, the commander knows where the position is, then it is supposed to fortify the position and then I would come in and I would say, This is okay, this is not okay, commander, sir, can we maybe make some changes here, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And the AOR, I believe you've testified that the AOR of the 5th Battalion was from around Paljenik to Malovan Greda. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our area of responsibility held by our battalion was from the right-hand side of Paljenik and then over to Malovan Greda. That was the area that we held with our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately -- well, the area of that responsibility is about two kilometres, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. I never measured it, but that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm just asking for your approximation. And approximately how far is Kesten from Malovan Greda?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it takes about 20 minutes to get down from Malovan Greda because you don't take a detour. When we went down we went down in a straight line towards Kesten.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So that's 20 minutes by walking?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now we looked at a document yesterday which is Exhibit 466 and from this document I asked to you mark some places on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And we can bring up that document, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But do you recall the document that mentioned the El Mujahedin being used or being on standby as an intervention in a certain area, including the Kesten village?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of this unit that was operating approximately 20 minutes from the front line of your unit?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of them operating there, because I didn't know what units of were actually operating there. As I said, those meetings were held by the commanders, and they decided and they did not relay their decisions to us, it would be this unit there, that unit somewhere else. We had our own area of responsibility and let me repeat, we were part of the defensive system. Once the defence line moved, then we would take that. We would simply man the new positions that had been taken initially by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, on the 10th of September, do you have any knowledge of where the 2nd Manoeuvre Battalion operated?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to where any other units that were in the 35th Division operated?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who operated where and who was included. I only told you what was held by the battalions. As for what units participated, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And by -- when you say "battalions," can you tell us -- "I only told you what was held by the battalions," not sure I recall that. Can you tell us again what was held by which battalions?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the battalions in that area of responsibility next to us. It was the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and we were the 5th. We held the defence lines. As for who participated in the operation, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour? Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just for some clarification, when you just mentioned 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, now, with regard to the 2nd is that the 2nd Manoeuvre Battalion that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the battalion of the 328th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Sartorio. Mr. Robson, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've just been asked about Exhibit 466, which was a document from the 35th Division dated 10th of September, 1995, and it mentioned the locations of Kesten, Kosa and Prokop. Prior to coming to The Hague, had you ever seen that order before?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of whether the El Mujahedin Detachment received that order?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How would I know that? I don't know why I was asked the question or to mark those locations. I wasn't there. As one of Their Honours noted, it could have been marked down by anyone. I don't know why I was asked for that location, since I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. You were also asked some questions about the statements that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor. When you were interviewed by an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006, do you remember what term you used to describe the men, the 20 or so men, that came into the Dom when you were taking down the names of the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that a group of Arabs arrived. Then he asked me whether it was the El Mujahid Unit. I said I don't know, and then he insisted - excuse me - that it was the El Mujahid Unit, since it was the only unit there, as he said, meaning that it could have been -- it could have not been anyone else. I also didn't know whether there were any other units, save for the El Mujahid Unit, and I consented to what he said, following his assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Did the investigator act fairly when he insisted upon using the term "El Mujahedin Unit"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Isn't that for the Court to decide?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll leave it for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You were asked about four VRS soldiers that were taken by Arabs earlier on during the 10th of September, 1995. You told us that you were told about this information about Mr. Sogolj. Can you tell us, where were you exactly when Mr. Sogolj told you about those four VRS soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the Kesten hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: At that point in time, were you aware that there were 51 Serb prisoners of war inside the Dom?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I did not. First, he told me what was going on, he told me there were some captured persons. However, he didn't specify what the number was. I said what I said. He told me that three women had been captured as well as two children, and after he told me all that, I went inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You've told us that you did find out that there were Serb POWs inside the Dom. Would it have been possible for you to go off and investigate what had happened to the four Serb POWs captured earlier that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no possibility to investigate that. If I turned to anyone, they would probably have asked me what I was doing there and under what authority I was acting. If someone was captured by anyone, they were supposed to take care of that. They would probably ask me, Who are you to come here from the 5th Battalion to try and investigate this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now we know that you took a list of the names of the 51 prisoners of war inside the Dom, and on the 11th of September, you prepared a further list that we've seen as an exhibit during the course of your evidence. On that list, you mentioned the words "4 Arapi," and you explained to us the meaning of those words. When you sent your report to Mr. Malicbegovic, the assistant commander for security in the 328th Brigade, did you mention in that report that four Serb prisoners of war had been captured earlier during the day?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned that. I wrote down that in that area, four captured persons were observed. I wrote down what I was told by the commander of the 2nd Mountain Company. He told me that four soldiers were seen being taken away by the Arabs. The list was merely there to provide information it contained. However, the other document sent alongside the report was expanded, including all of the events, since I wasn't able to write all that down originally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in the report to Mr. Malicbegovic, did you also mention that two children had been released?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then, finally, you told us that on the 10th of September, when you found out what had happened -- when you found out that there were Serb prisoners of war in the Dom at Kesten, you informed your commander, and he told you that he would be sending military policemen to Kesten. In your view was there anything else that you could have reasonably done that day?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I informed my commander, it was his duty to pass it on, and he did. He informed the brigade. They have their own military police battalions, do not, meaning that it was up to the brigade to do something. I thought that these were merely prisoners who had been disarmed, probably had surrendered. I thought there would be no resistance and that the few men I had were sufficient to provide security, and before the prisoners were taken over by the military police. They were supposed to provide means of transport. I believe the truck was supposed to be sent to transport them, since Zavidovici is rather far from Kesten. It was impossible for them to walk.
