When the incident took place, I couldn't do anything. I believe I did everything I could. I avoided any firing, any killings. I saved the lives of myself and those of my soldiers and the captured people. Had I done anything else, and as I said, I did not wear any weapons throughout the war, since we were short on weapons, meaning that commanders and assistant commanders did not have weapons. The three or four soldiers did, and when Muhamed came in, he did not have any weapons either. Had I done anything, say, to shoot them or anything, they would have probably been able to kill one or two Arabs, but that would have been it. All of us would have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually I do have a few questions. First, one to Madam Sartorio, because we are still left with the exhibit 1353, and I'm not sure that I understood the reason why these extra names had to be pointed out on the map. You promised, us, Madam Sartorio, that you would get back to the map so as to explain to us why you had asked the witness to point out these areas for us. And I'm asking because if you don't explain that, then I think we should just not admit the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I -- for reasons -- we'll just keep the map either marked for identification or withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Your choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we just to keep it marked, Your Honour, if we could -- may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will then keep it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, one little question about the ID cards that were gathered from the 51 Serb prisoners in the hall in Kesten. Do you know what became of those identity cards afterwards?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only IDs. There were military booklets there, health insurance cards, any documents found with the prisoners were on -- in a single pile. I put it all in a bag and it stayed with me until the next day when I drafted the report on the 11th. I sent the bag together with the report to my superior, the assistant commander at the level of the brigade. After that, when we met at a brigade meeting, I remember seeing those documents in the assistant's office. Therefore, I know they reached him, but I don't know what he did with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, I just wanted to -- one issue I'd like to raise with you but before I raise the issue, let me just explain to you that I understand that you said you -- when you got to the hall in Kesten you did call for transport to come and pick up your -- these prisoners; I understand that. My question relates to the next stage. When the Arabs took or ordered you out of the building and took possession of these prisoners of war forcibly, did you do anything, did you report this to your superiors, to ask for backup, to come -- because these prisoners of war were your responsibility. I'm talking about the 51, not the four.

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said I had informed my commander. He knew what was going on, and he said they were to come to Kesten and -- so he did. I cannot command troops. I cannot order troops. That was supposed to be done by the commander or someone similar, who had the power of command. In terms of my position, I couldn't order soldiers to do this or that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, okay, sorry, sir. We don't have much time. Don't go and explaining to lots of things. I haven't asked you whether you had -- you could command troops. I'm asking whether you could -- you did -- you did ask for help from your commander, backup, then he can order the troops to come and help you to take these prisoners away from these Arabs. Did you do that? Did you ask for that assistance, as the person responsible for the security of these prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed my commander that a group of Arabs took them away by force. I didn't know what to do next, and I didn't know what he -- what steps he was to take. I just told him that they were taken away from the Kesten hall. He said he would arrive there to see. As for what he did, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, any questions arising, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you about ID cards and you said at a brigade meeting you remember seeing those documents in the assistant's office. Just so we're clear, whose office was it in which you saw those ID cards?

utterances.speaker: IZET KARAHASANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the assistant commander for security of the 328th, Enes Malicbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, that brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time off to come and testify at the Tribunal. I hope you have a safe trip back home. You are now excused. You may now stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we had informed you, we decided not to call Mrs. Saracevic who was supposed to appear today. I believe we advised you of that early this week as well as the Prosecutor's office. We have no further witnesses therefor, since we couldn't find any replacements, given that those other witnesses are supposed to testify longer, and that, in turn, would mean that any witnesses would have to stay for at least three or four days. The witnesses we have for the next two weeks were also quite occupied with other matters and none of them were unable to arrive today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. With respect to that correspondence from the Italian, government, we're trying to get it translated so that we can tell the parties what it says. And now that you are saying that we are -- you don't have any other witness, I don't know whether you would like to come back at the next session to hear what they said or you prefer to hear what the correspondence says at the next hearing on the date to which we will postpone. I think you, Madam Vidovic, it is an urgent matter on your side. You've got to tell us how urgent it is that you know what the content of the letter says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a very urgent matter for us. I'm afraid if we wait another few days, it will put us in a situation that we don't know what the result is going to be and we'll have to worry about when we will be getting the documents to translate them. As you could see from our motion, we asked the Bench to be able to show those to another witness, and this would disturb the entire plan we had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. We will then --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I have another, Your Honour. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I knew you were just going to say we're adjourned and that's why, I apologise for interrupting. We do have one matter we'd like to raise, Your Honour, with respect to an exhibit that was admitted with this last witness, so may I be heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: With respect to exhibit 651 which was the typed list of names, I'm not sure if Your Honours recall but the Defence attempted to get in this document through witness Goran Krcmar, who was -- testified on the 26th of October, and this witness renounced any -- this document, and as a result of that, Your Honours did not admit the document and subsequent do that testimony, we filed a motion on the 7th of November to -- for leave to amend the exhibit list to add documents which we believe cast doubt on the validity of that list and was contained -- some of the information that's contained in that document. We would like to -- those documents -- there are 13 documents and they are on my exhibit list for this witness but obviously this witness can't testify about these documents, they are correspondence between the Office of the Prosecutor, counsel for the Defence, the BiH, the Republika Srpska government, and there's 13 documents and back-and-forth discussion about that exhibit 651 and the ultimate result is P06240 and it explains some of the discrepancies and what we argue invalidates some of the information contained in that document. So we would like to move to admit those documents from the bar table, either orally today for if you prefer we can file a written motion. But we think it is important that have you these documents and the Defence has had these documents. The Defence knows what is the Prosecution's position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know how the Chamber would -- is in a position to assess whether to admit or not admit because we haven't seen those documents, including P06240.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: They were attached to the motion that we asked to amount the exhibit list so they -- there are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but I'm not sure -- I don't know what it is -- what are the 13 documents that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, again I can resubmit this. Instead of a motion to amend it will be a motion to admit but it will be virtually the same argument but there is a list, there is an annex, an appendix which describes each of the documents. Each of the documents is attached to the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic, you were on your feet?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was about to ask about something I overheard when you seem to have forgotten to turn the microphone off. I believe the Prosecutor is bound to submit a written motion since we have numerous arguments that we want to put forth concerning the possibility of exhibits being admitted at this late stage of the Defence case, given the Rule 85, which defines strictly the possibility of presentation of evidence and admitting of exhibits as well as describing the procedure. Therefore, we ask that the Prosecutor submit a written motion; if not, I am quite ready to present oral arguments countering their request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I wish I knew what it is you overheard that I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would suggest that you file a written motion specifically for those 13 documents, Madam Sartorio, and let's whatever you want -- whether it is an amendment or admission, whatever you want to call it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You don't have to tell me. I just wish I knew, but I don't want to you tell me. Thank you very much. We'll then have to take an adjournment, and I'm being advised that we're adjourning to the 8th of April. Indeed, at quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II, 8th of April. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I was under the impression that the Defence wanted to the know the translation of the Italian document and we were going to hopefully get that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll then come back at half past 12.00. We will take our normal break up until half past 12.00 to give the translator to finish, and then we will reconvene at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.
